text:
I am standing on the platform of the railway carriage. I have stood there all night,
wrapped in my cloak. I have watched the evening shadows creep up from the valleys
along the mountains, until everything was shrouded in darkness. Now day is drawing
near, a pale glow brightens on the horizon; with ever quicker piston strokes, in
time with my heart, the train rushes onward toward the foreign city.

What strange unrest has kept me awake the whole night? What anxious questions are
these for which my heart seeks answers, while I stare broodingly out into the
darkness?

I cannot, after all, doubt Maria’s love; I no longer doubt my own.

Yet I journey trembling to our meeting. For my anxious question is this: Might we
not feel like strangers to one another?

The Maria whom I am travelling out to find is not the Maria of before. She is
not the recklessly enamoured child who in the old days laid herself in my arms,
not the cheerful and ever-ready mistress, my conquest and my prize—she is surely
both the one and the other, but at the same time something greater and higher,
that which perhaps was always the background of her nature, that which I thought
I sensed the last times we were together, that which, in the final reckoning,
became the Madonna image of my solitary worship.

And she—will she recognise me? I scarcely do so myself. I won her in play; I took
her sword in hand. Every day the dance we danced was so easy. And now I come to
her with unarmed earnestness. Before, it was a matter of a dance; now, it is a
matter of life. Before, in rich high spirits, I contented myself with little; now,
in poor humility, I ask for Everything.

... We speed onward toward the dawning morning. Suddenly it is black night once
more: amid thundering noise the train hurtles through a tunnel. The darkness
presses against my chest, there is a rushing in my ears, and, dizzy, I grasp the
platform railing. It seems to me that this tunnel will never end; I grope my way
forward to reach the lighted carriage—when ... what a revelation! At the purple
rim of the sky the disc of the sun rises, spreading its golden halo far and wide,
pouring trembling, warm light over moistly gleaming grassy valleys and slopes of
grain.

Beautiful, fair Day, with joyful gratitude I kneel before You, You who delivered
me from my agonising Night and led me, with faith reborn, to Maria.




LXI.


The golden sun of reunion over mountains, the glittering tears of reunion in
silent valleys.

In wondering rapture we stand facing one another, unable to find words, unable
to ask, unable to answer, able only to sink into one another’s arms and, rejoicing,
weeping, in shared bliss praise the rising Day.

Was it truly no dream? Was it truly You and me? We look at one another; we shake
our heads in disbelief. And yet only now, it seems to us, do we truly know one
another. For this is the sublime miracle of our reunion: we meet as so often
before we met in the happy dream of our scarcely confessed longing. Now the dream
is living and breathing.

And You, lovely, living, breathing girl, with the quiet happiness of transfiguration
in your roguish eyes, with a woman’s mature thoughtfulness upon your child’s
brow, You put your arms around my neck and You say: “So at last it has happened,
at the eleventh hour, but not too late—that for which I never ceased to hope. For
it is true, is it not? Not something You will regret tomorrow, not something You
are imagining now because You have longed a little for your mistress?”

I answer: “As surely as I have always preferred to tell You too little rather than
too much, so surely do I love You. I love You in joy and in distress, on weekdays
and feast days. You are the one with whom I wish to die, but first I wish to live
with You for a very, very long time. Indeed, I have longed for my lovely mistress’s
caresses. But most of all I have longed for all the rest that is also You: your
faithful heart, your pure thought, your gentle speech, your bright smile, which
is my sun in doubt, your good handclasp, which is my strength upon the road.”

But when I tell Maria this, she weeps because she understands that I am speaking
the truth, and because she is happy.




LXII.


Someone tugs me from behind by the sleeve. I am sitting with Maria on my lap and
say angrily: “Who dares disturb us?”

But a voice whispers: “I come as a deputation from the readers. Your book, which
was dreadful at the beginning, has gradually taken a better course. There are
even some among us who have had tears in their eyes. But now we are so afraid that
in the end it will nevertheless go astray. For God’s sake: surely you intend to
marry Maria? Remember, you have taken her from her suitor, who had the most
respectable intentions?”

My stern lady censor, do not be afraid. Maria, tell the kind lady that she may
leave us alone without any scruples.




LXIII.


The Bishop stands before the altar in his golden vestment, shining in rivalry
with the candelabra. The venerable marble statues in the niches have been washed,
and at the organ sits the venerable old Master, with a silk skullcap on his head
and the Grand Cross upon his breast.

The pews are filled with the country’s most enamoured young women and men. They
have flowers in their hands; they sit in pairs, the young women with white roses,
the young men with red. They all stare down toward the entrance door, where twelve
kindly old priests in black velvet robes stand arrayed, six on either side.

Then the Master begins to play. The tones of the organ surge beneath the lofty
vaults. The young women and men rise.

The heavy oak door is flung open; a dazzling light fills the opening: there stands
Maria in her white bridal gown, surrounded by the billowing folds of the long
veil. A blushing maiden with downcast eyes. Heavenly majesty, blessed happiness
radiate from her.

A murmur of admiration passes through the church; the Bishop at the altar turns,
puts on his spectacles, and when he sees how lovely Maria is, he hastens to meet
her, bows to her, and leads her by the hand to the altar.

The young women and men scatter their roses, the red and the white, over her as
she passes; some of the roses remain caught in the veil, and Maria smiles when
she sees the flower-strewn gown.

But the old Master has stopped playing; he leans out over the balustrade of the
organ loft to see Maria, and curious angels’ faces peer through the apertures in
the vaults.

... Then, with the words of the Old and New Testaments, Maria is given into my
hand; I lead her out, followed by the Bishop and the twelve priests, as well as
all the enamoured young couples, while the old Master plays with one hand and
waves to us with the other.

Outside, the carriage with the white horses is waiting, and we climb in to drive
home to me, home to us. And then the bells begin to peal.
